items.title: Four labs find experimental differences can undermine AI catalyst predictions
items.excerpt: A four-laboratory round-robin led by SLAC found that tiny procedural differences — above all mixing intensity — produced inconsistent catalyst measurements, meaning the datasets used to train materials ML models can encode lab artifacts rather than chemistry. The authors argue standardized protocols and metadata are a precondition for AI-driven catalysis.

items.title: AI models atom movement to predict solid-state reaction pathways, including impurities, in minutes
items.excerpt: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory researchers built an AI model that predicts how solid-state chemical reactions actually proceed by accounting for atomic diffusion, returning likely pathways and impurity phases in minutes instead of months of trial-and-error synthesis.

items.title: Seven possible quasar lenses emerge from AI scan of 800,000 DESI objects
items.excerpt: Ohio State astronomers trained a neural network on simulated imagery and turned it loose on 800,000 Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument objects, surfacing seven candidate gravitationally lensed quasars — roughly doubling the known sample of these rare cosmological rulers.

items.title: Noninvasive AI-based system translates brain signals into written text
items.excerpt: Researchers built a noninvasive brain-computer interface that decodes typed sentences from EEG and MEG recordings using a deep learning decoder, hitting a 29% character error rate with MEG and as low as 18% for the best participants — no implant required.

items.title: Standardized battery database could improve AI-guided solid-state battery design
items.excerpt: University of Maryland researchers released an open-access database of 245 solid-state battery records with standardized reporting fields, aiming to give machine learning models the consistent, comparable training data that scattered literature values have so far denied them.

items.title: Adaptive decision support can fight overreliance on AI
items.excerpt: Harvard SEAS researchers used reinforcement learning to build an assistant that decides in the moment how much to help each person, rather than always volunteering a recommendation. In experiments the adaptive policy preserved human skill and judgment better than constant AI suggestions.

items.title: Solving the solvent problem
items.excerpt: An AI-guided algorithm generated 100,000 candidate solvent molecules, which MIT researchers narrowed to 200 and then synthesized, finding that shrinking solvent size breaks the usual trade-off between ion transport speed and electrolyte stability in sodium-metal batteries.

items.title: The benefits of medical AI assistance vary based on user expertise
items.excerpt: In an MIT study of skin-disease diagnosis, AI assistance raised accuracy for both clinicians and non-experts — but non-experts deferred to the model even when it was wrong, while clinicians more often caught its mistakes. Expertise, not the model, determined who benefited.

items.title: Science One Framework: A verifiable autonomous research framework via Chain-of-Evidence
items.excerpt: Google Research introduced Science One, an autonomous research framework that natively builds verifiable evidence chains behind every claim an AI system makes. In their evaluation the approach cut phantom-reference rates in AI-generated scientific papers from 21% to zero.

items.title: Towards a quantum computer that learns from its errors
items.excerpt: Google Research showed reinforcement learning agents that retune quantum control parameters live, without halting computation, so a processor can adapt to hardware drift. The work sits alongside neural decoders like AlphaQubit in the push toward self-correcting quantum machines.

items.title: The OlmoEarth Platform: Geospatial inference at planetary scale
items.excerpt: Ai2 detailed the infrastructure behind OlmoEarth, letting researchers fine-tune geospatial foundation models and run continent-scale satellite inference in about a day at fractions of a penny per square kilometer — turning Earth-observation science into a routine query.

items.title: Are AI scribes useful tools in medical education, or a crutch that imperils learning?
items.excerpt: Medical schools are debating whether to restrict AI scribes during training, worried that automating note-writing removes the cognitive work that builds diagnostic reasoning. "The process of deliberately crafting the note forces us to use our brains," one educator argues.

items.title: We lead the Federation of State Medical Boards. Here's what we think about licensing AI to practice medicine
items.excerpt: The Federation of State Medical Boards argues AI should be governed as a tool inside existing accountability structures rather than licensed as an independent practitioner, since a medical license is "not just a permit to generate thoughtful and informed answers."

items.title: AI Uses MRIs to Generate Brain Aging Maps for Neurodegenerative Disease Research
items.excerpt: USC researchers trained an AI model on nearly 15,000 MRI scans to produce regional brain-aging maps, revealing that different brain regions age at very different rates — a finer-grained signal than a single brain-age number for spotting early neurodegeneration.

items.title: Your AI calorie-tracking app may be off by 345 calories
items.excerpt: An American Society for Nutrition study tested popular AI-powered food-photo apps and found they can miss a large share of a meal, underestimating intake by hundreds of calories — a caution about treating consumer computer vision as measurement-grade data.

items.title: A Clinician's Field Guide to Vetting AI Mental Health Tools
items.excerpt: A practical six-question framework for clinicians evaluating AI mental health chatbots — covering legal status, crisis recognition, escalation behavior and data privacy — as therapy bots proliferate faster than the evidence base behind them.

items.title: How AI helps scientists design the next generation of medicines
items.excerpt: Away from the generative-AI spotlight, machine learning models are compressing drug-development timelines by rapidly triaging molecular candidates and opening previously "undruggable" targets, with closed-loop AI-plus-robotics discovery labs now being built to match.
